rows.subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager notices sideways glances at school and reads gossip or judgement, though people also look away from shyness or thought. Assuming the worst can cause needless conflict, so checking the facts helps.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager's cheeks rise in a real smile or redden from embarrassment, and either can be hard to control. Others read the state from context, and kindness spares a teenager who blushes.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager wrinkles the nose at something unpleasant but learns to soften the reaction to avoid hurting a friend. Being honest in words, kindly, is better than a silent sneer.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Lip biting when unsure or anxious [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager bites the lip to stay quiet, hold back words or calm nerves. It signals restraint, and noticing it in a friend may open a gentle question.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Pouting and pursing for cameras and moods [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager pouts or purses the lips in a selfie as a style, or in real sulking. The difference lies in context, and mocking a genuine sulk can deepen hurt.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager clenches the jaw in exams or arguments to hold back words, showing tension. Slow breathing and stretching the jaw help, and adults can offer to talk without pressure.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: relief from stress

rows.subtype: Moving the jaw sideways and tongue clicks [Mismatch]
rows.description: A teenager shifts the jaw sideways or clicks the tongue when thinking or being dismissive, which peers may take as attitude. The meaning depends on tone and relationship.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager holds a still face to seem cool or hide nerves, while another has a resting face that looks unfriendly. Neither is proof of coldness, so asking helps.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Tense or rigid face under threat [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager notices a friend's rigid, frozen face after upsetting news and understands it may mean shock or fear, not indifference. Quiet support and time are better than demanding a reaction.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager meeting people in India sees the side-to-side head wobble, which can mean yes, okay, I understand or I am listening depending on the tilt and context. It is not a clear no, so ask if unsure.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26
